title: Atomic Physics and X-rays

toc.title: 19.1 Bohr's theory of the hydrogen atom: energy levels and spectral series
19.2 de Broglie waves and the uncertainty principle
19.3 X-rays: production, properties and uses; Bragg's law

html:
Modern Physics carries 12 of the 50 Physics questions (official MEC weightage), and we estimate about 2 come from this chapter. They are almost always one Bohr-model calculation — an orbit radius, an energy, a wavelength or a series name — and one X-ray fact, usually the Duane–Hunt limit \lambda_{min} = hc/eV or Bragg's law. Both halves reward a small number of remembered results, and both punish the two standard confusions: putting the Lyman series in the visible, and calling the K_\alpha line the shortest wavelength in the X-ray spectrum.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Bohr's three postulates, and the quantisation condition mvr = nh/2\pi.
  • The hydrogen results: r_n \propto n^2, v_n \propto 1/n, E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV.
  • The five named series, the level each ends on, and the region each lies in.
  • Ionisation energy 13.6 eV; first excitation 10.2 eV; the Rydberg formula.
  • de Broglie's relation \lambda = h/p and the uncertainty principle, as statements with one consequence.
  • X-ray production, the continuous and characteristic spectra, \lambda_{min} = hc/eV.
  • Bragg's law 2d\sin\theta = n\lambda and Moseley's law qualitatively.

19.1 Bohr's theory of the hydrogen atom: energy levels and spectral series

Why the Rutherford atom had to be replaced

Rutherford's experiment (1911) put a tiny positive nucleus at the centre of the atom, with electrons outside it. That picture has a fatal flaw in classical physics. An electron moving in a circle is accelerating, and an accelerating charge radiates energy. So the electron should lose energy continuously, spiral into the nucleus in about 10^{-11} s, and the light it emitted should form a continuous spectrum that changes as the orbit shrinks.

Neither happens. Atoms are stable, and a hydrogen discharge emits a spectrum of sharp lines — a few fixed wavelengths, not a smear. Niels Bohr (1913) kept the nuclear model and added three postulates that remove both contradictions.

Bohr's postulates
  1. Stationary states. An electron can revolve round the nucleus only in certain allowed orbits, and while it is in one of them it does not radiate, even though it is accelerating.
  2. Quantisation of angular momentum. The allowed orbits are those for which the angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h/2\pi: mvr = nh/2\pi, n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
  3. Quantum jumps. Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron moves between two allowed orbits, and one photon carries the whole energy difference: hf = E_2 - E_1.

The integer n is the principal quantum number. The orbit with n = 1 is the ground state; n = 2, 3, \dots are excited states.

The radius, speed and energy

The electron of charge -e moves in a circle of radius r round a nucleus of charge +e. The Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force.

The Bohr radius and the hydrogen energy levels

Setting up. Let m be the electron mass, v its speed, r the orbit radius, and k = 1/4\pi\varepsilon_0. Two equations hold: force balance and angular-momentum quantisation.

Step 1 — force balance. The Coulomb force is the centripetal force:

\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{ke^2}{r^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad mv^2 = \frac{ke^2}{r}

Step 2 — quantisation. From mvr = nh/2\pi, the speed is v = nh/(2\pi mr).

Step 3 — substitute. Squaring the speed and putting it into Step 1:

\frac{m n^2h^2}{4\pi^2m^2r^2} = \frac{ke^2}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_n = \frac{n^2h^2}{4\pi^2 m k e^2}

Step 4 — put in the numbers. With h = 6.63\times10^{-34} J s, m = 9.11\times10^{-31} kg, e = 1.6\times10^{-19} C and k = 9\times10^9 N m² C⁻², the bracket is 0.529\times10^{-10} m. So

r_n = 0.529\,n^2 \ \text{Å} = a_0n^2

where a_0 = 0.529 Å is the Bohr radius.

Step 5 — the speed. Putting r_n back into v = nh/(2\pi mr) gives

v_n = \frac{e^2}{2\varepsilon_0nh} = \frac{2.19\times10^6}{n}\ \text{m s}^{-1}

Step 6 — the energy. Kinetic energy K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = ke^2/2r; potential energy U = -ke^2/r. So U = -2K and

E_n = K + U = -\frac{ke^2}{2r_n} = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}\ \text{eV}

Result. r_n \propto n^2, v_n \propto 1/n, E_n \propto -1/n^2, with E_1 = -13.6 eV.

What it means. The negative sign means the electron is bound: 13.6 eV must be supplied to remove it from the ground state. The energy levels crowd together as n grows and reach zero at n = \infty, where the electron is free.

Quantity in state n Depends on n as Ground-state value
Radius r_n n^2 0.529 Å
Speed v_n 1/n 2.19\times10^6 m s⁻¹
Kinetic energy K_n 1/n^2 13.6 eV
Potential energy U_n -1/n^2 −27.2 eV
Total energy E_n -1/n^2 −13.6 eV
Angular momentum L_n n h/2\pi
Time period T_n n^3 1.5\times10^{-16} s

Note the useful pair U = 2E and K = -E: the potential energy is twice the total energy, and the kinetic energy is minus the total energy. In the ground state K = 13.6 eV, U = -27.2 eV, E = -13.6 eV.

The two energies students mix up

Ionisation energy is the energy to take the electron from its present level to n = \infty: 13.6 eV from the ground state, but only 3.4 eV from n = 2. Excitation energy is the energy to lift it to the next level: 10.2 eV from n = 1 to n = 2, and 12.09 eV from n = 1 to n = 3. An electron in the ground state cannot absorb a photon of 12 eV — photons are absorbed whole, and 12 eV matches no gap. It can absorb 10.2 eV, 12.09 eV, 12.75 eV, … exactly.

The spectral series

A downward jump from level n_2 to a lower level n_1 emits a photon of energy 13.6(1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2) eV. In wavelength form this is the Rydberg formula:

\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right), \qquad R = 1.097\times10^7\ \text{m}^{-1}

with n_2 > n_1. Each fixed n_1 gives a series; within a series n_2 runs from n_1 + 1 upward, and the lines crowd together towards the series limit at n_2 = \infty, where \lambda_{limit} = 1/(R/n_1^2).

Series Ends on n_1 Region First line \lambda Series limit
Lyman 1 ultraviolet 121.6 nm (Ly-α) 91.2 nm
Balmer 2 visible (and near UV) 656.3 nm (Hα, red) 364.6 nm
Paschen 3 infrared 1875 nm 820 nm
Brackett 4 infrared 4050 nm 1458 nm
Pfund 5 infrared 7460 nm 2279 nm

The visible hydrogen lines all belong to the Balmer series: Hα (656 nm, red), Hβ (486 nm, blue-green), Hγ (434 nm, violet) and Hδ (410 nm, violet). The series limit of Balmer, 364.6 nm, is the shortest wavelength the series can reach.

The series in order

Lyman Balmer Paschen Brackett Pfund — “Little Boys Play Basketball Perfectly”. The ending level is the position in the list: Lyman 1, Balmer 2, Paschen 3, Brackett 4, Pfund 5.

Number of lines. An electron falling from level n can take any downward jump, and each pair of levels gives one line. The number of possible lines is

N = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}

so a gas of atoms in the n = 4 state can emit 6 different wavelengths.

Worked example 19.1 — the red line of hydrogen

Problem. Find the energy and wavelength of the photon emitted when a hydrogen atom drops from n = 3 to n = 2.

Solution. E = 13.6(1/2^2 - 1/3^2) = 13.6(1/4 - 1/9) = 1.89 eV. Using 1240\ \text{eV nm} = hc: \lambda = 1240/1.89 = 656 nm — the red Hα line, in the visible.

Worked example 19.2 — ionising an excited atom

Problem. A hydrogen atom is in the n = 2 state. What is the longest wavelength that can ionise it?

Solution. Ionisation from n = 2 needs 0 - (-3.4) = 3.4 eV. The longest wavelength corresponds to exactly this energy: \lambda = 1240/3.4 = 365 nm — the Balmer limit, in the near ultraviolet. Any photon of 365 nm or shorter will do; a longer one cannot.

Successes and limits of the Bohr model

Bohr's model gets the hydrogen spectrum exactly right, explains why atoms are stable, predicts the correct ionisation energy, and gives the right size for the atom. It fails for everything with more than one electron (helium onward), cannot explain the relative brightness of spectral lines, says nothing about fine structure or the splitting of lines in a magnetic field (the Zeeman effect), and assumes sharp circular orbits that quantum mechanics does not allow. It is a half-way house: correct energies, wrong picture.

19.2 de Broglie waves and the uncertainty principle

Matter waves

In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed that if light waves can behave as particles (photons, Chapter 18), then particles should behave as waves. A particle of momentum p = mv has a de Broglie wavelength

\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}

For a particle of kinetic energy K (non-relativistic), p = \sqrt{2mK}, so

\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}

For an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference V, K = eV and

\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{150}{V}}\ \text{Å}

with V in volts. At 100 V the wavelength is 1.23 Å — about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why electrons diffract from crystals.

Object Speed de Broglie wavelength
Electron, 100 V 5.9\times10^6 m s⁻¹ 1.23 Å
Electron, 10 kV 5.9\times10^7 m s⁻¹ 0.123 Å
Proton, same 100 V 1.4\times10^5 m s⁻¹ 2.9\times10^{-12} m
Cricket ball, 0.16 kg 30 m s⁻¹ 1.4\times10^{-34} m

The last line is the important one. A cricket ball has a wavelength 10^{20} times smaller than a nucleus, so no experiment can detect its wave nature. Wave behaviour matters only when \lambda is comparable to the size of the obstacles or openings in the experiment — for electrons in crystals, for neutrons in diffraction experiments, for atoms in interferometers.

The first evidence came from Davisson and Germer (1927): a beam of electrons reflected from a nickel crystal produced a diffraction pattern with maxima at angles given by Bragg's law, exactly as waves would. Electron microscopes are the practical application: a 100 kV electron has \lambda \approx 0.004 nm, thousands of times shorter than visible light, so the resolution is thousands of times better.

Bohr's orbits explained. A de Broglie wave going round an orbit must fit a whole number of wavelengths, otherwise it cancels itself: 2\pi r = n\lambda = nh/mv. Rearranged, mvr = nh/2\pi — Bohr's quantisation condition is just the condition for a standing wave round the nucleus.

Worked example 19.3 — electron wavelength

Problem. Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V.

Solution. K = eV = 1.6\times10^{-17} J. p = \sqrt{2mK} = \sqrt{2(9.11\times10^{-31})(1.6\times10^{-17})} = 5.4\times10^{-24} kg m s⁻¹. \lambda = h/p = 6.63\times10^{-34}/5.4\times10^{-24} = 1.2\times10^{-10} m = 1.2 Å. (The shortcut \sqrt{150/100} = 1.22 Å gives the same.)

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

A wave does not have a sharp position, so a particle described by a matter wave cannot have both a sharp position and a sharp momentum. Heisenberg (1927) made this precise:

Uncertainty principle

\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \frac{h}{4\pi} = \frac{\hbar}{2}

The product of the uncertainties in position and momentum of a particle can never be smaller than h/4\pi. There is a companion relation between energy and time,

\Delta E\,\Delta t \ge \frac{h}{4\pi}

Here \hbar = h/2\pi = 1.055\times10^{-34} J s. The principle is not a statement about clumsy instruments; it is a property of nature. Measuring the position precisely (small \Delta x) forces a large spread of momentum, and vice versa.

An order-of-magnitude consequence. Confine an electron to a region the size of an atom, \Delta x \approx 10^{-10} m. Then

\Delta p \ge \frac{1.055\times10^{-34}}{2\times10^{-10}} = 5.3\times10^{-25}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}, \qquad \Delta v \ge \frac{\Delta p}{m_e} \approx 6\times10^5\ \text{m s}^{-1}

That is the same order as the electron's orbital speed. So an electron in an atom cannot be pictured as a particle moving along a definite path; only a probability cloud has meaning. Confine the same electron to a nucleus (\Delta x \approx 10^{-14} m) and the minimum speed becomes 6\times10^9 m s⁻¹ — greater than the speed of light. Electrons cannot exist inside nuclei; the electrons emitted in beta decay are created at the moment of decay.

What the principle does and does not say

It does not say that a particle has a definite position and momentum that we simply do not know. It says the pair has no simultaneous definite values. It also does not stop us measuring one of them exactly — only both at once. And \Delta E \Delta t \ge \hbar/2 explains the natural width of spectral lines: a state that lives only 10^{-8} s has an energy uncertain by about 10^{-7} eV.

19.3 X-rays: production, properties and uses; Bragg's law

The Coolidge tube

X-rays are produced when fast electrons strike a heavy metal target. In a modern Coolidge tube:

  • a tungsten filament (cathode) is heated by a small current and emits electrons by thermionic emission;
  • a high voltage (typically 20–150 kV) accelerates these electrons towards the anode, a heavy metal such as tungsten or molybdenum;
  • the tube is evacuated, so the electrons travel without colliding with gas;
  • more than 99 % of the electron energy becomes heat in the anode, which is therefore cooled (often a rotating anode spreads the heat).

The tube current (filament heating) controls the number of electrons, hence the intensity of the X-rays. The tube voltage controls the energy of each electron, hence the penetrating power (hardness) and the shortest wavelength.

The two spectra

An X-ray tube emits a superposition of two distinct spectra.

1. Continuous spectrum (bremsstrahlung). An electron passing close to a nucleus is decelerated and radiates the lost energy as a photon. The energy lost can be anything from zero up to the whole kinetic energy eV, so the spectrum is continuous. The most energetic photon occurs when the electron loses all its energy in one collision:

\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}

This is the Duane–Hunt limit. It depends only on the tube voltage, not on the target metal.

2. Characteristic spectrum. If the bombarding electron knocks out an inner (K-shell) electron, an electron from a higher shell falls down and emits a photon of fixed energy. These are the sharp K-series lines: K_\alpha (from L to K) and K_\beta (from M to K). Their wavelengths are a fingerprint of the target element and do not change when the tube voltage changes (as long as the voltage is high enough to remove a K electron at all).

The K_\alpha trap

The K_\alpha line is not the shortest wavelength in the spectrum. The continuous cut-off \lambda_{min} is always shorter, because it comes from an electron losing all its energy at once, while K_\alpha comes from a transition with a fixed, smaller energy. In the figure the cut-off is at 0.035 nm and K_\alpha at 0.071 nm.

Properties of X-rays

Property Consequence
Electromagnetic waves, wavelength about 0.01–10 nm travel at c, obey reflection, refraction, diffraction, polarisation
No charge not deflected by electric or magnetic fields (unlike cathode rays)
High photon energy ionise gases, blacken photographic film, cause fluorescence
Penetrate matter absorbed more by dense, high-Z material (bone, lead) than by flesh
Produced by electron bombardment originate in the electron cloud, not the nucleus
Harmful to living tissue ionisation damages DNA; shielding and dose limits needed

Soft X-rays have long wavelength and low penetrating power; hard X-rays have short wavelength and high penetrating power. Raising the tube voltage makes the beam harder.

Uses

  • Diagnosis: radiographs of bone and teeth, mammography, CT scans, angiography. Absorption depends on density and atomic number, so bone (Z high) shows white against soft tissue.
  • Therapy: high-energy X-rays destroy cancer cells; the beam is aimed from several directions so the tumour receives a high dose and healthy tissue less.
  • Industry: checking welds and castings for internal cracks, scanning luggage.
  • Science: X-ray crystallography (Bragg), identifying elements by their characteristic lines (Moseley), X-ray fluorescence analysis.

Bragg's law

Crystals have layers of atoms separated by a distance d comparable to the X-ray wavelength. X-rays scattered from successive layers interfere. The ray from the second layer travels an extra distance 2d\sin\theta, where \theta is measured from the planes, not from the normal.

Bragg's law

2d\sin\theta = n\lambda

where d is the spacing between the reflecting planes, \theta the glancing angle between the ray and the plane, and n = 1, 2, 3, \dots the order of reflection.

Worked example 19.4 — a crystal spacing

Problem. X-rays of wavelength 0.154 nm are reflected from a crystal whose plane spacing is 0.282 nm. Find the glancing angle for the first-order maximum.

Solution. n = 1: \sin\theta = \lambda/(2d) = 0.154/(2\times0.282) = 0.273. \theta = \sin^{-1}(0.273) = 15.8^{\circ}.

Worked example 19.5 — the Duane–Hunt limit

Problem. An X-ray tube runs at 40 kV. Find the shortest wavelength emitted, and state what happens to it if the voltage is doubled.

Solution. \lambda_{min} = hc/eV = 1240\ \text{eV nm}/(4.0\times10^4\ \text{eV}) = 0.031 nm. Doubling the voltage doubles eV, so \lambda_{min} halves to 0.0155 nm. The target metal does not enter the calculation.

Moseley's law

Moseley (1913) measured the K_\alpha frequencies of many elements and found

\sqrt{f} = a(Z - b)

where Z is the atomic number, a is a constant and b \approx 1 for the K series. The frequency of the characteristic line therefore rises steadily with atomic number — the line is a fingerprint of the element. This is how Moseley established that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the real ordering number of the elements, and it is the basis of X-ray fluorescence identification. You are not expected to use the equation numerically, only to know that \sqrt{f} is linear in Z and that the line is characteristic of the element.

Formula and fact sheet

Quantity Formula or value
Angular momentum mvr = nh/2\pi, n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
Bohr radius r_n = 0.529\,n^2 Å; a_0 = 0.529 Å
Speed v_n = 2.19\times10^6/n m s⁻¹ = c/(137n)
Energy E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV = -2.18\times10^{-18}/n^2 J
Energy relations K = -E, U = 2E, U = -2K
Ionisation energy 13.6 eV from n=1; 13.6/n^2 eV from level n
Excitation 10.2 eV (1→2), 12.09 eV (1→3), 12.75 eV (1→4)
Rydberg 1/\lambda = R(1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2), R = 1.097\times10^7 m⁻¹
Photon energy shortcut E = 1240/\lambda with E in eV, \lambda in nm
Lines from level n n(n-1)/2
Series Lyman 1 (UV), Balmer 2 (visible), Paschen 3, Brackett 4, Pfund 5 (IR)
Balmer lines Hα 656 nm, Hβ 486 nm, Hγ 434 nm, Hδ 410 nm; limit 365 nm
Lyman limit 91.2 nm
de Broglie \lambda = h/p = h/mv = h/\sqrt{2mK}
Electron through V \lambda \approx \sqrt{150/V} Å
Uncertainty \Delta x\Delta p \ge h/4\pi; \Delta E\Delta t \ge h/4\pi
X-ray cut-off \lambda_{min} = hc/eV = 1240/V nm with V in volts
Bragg 2d\sin\theta = n\lambda (\theta from the planes)
Moseley \sqrt{f} = a(Z - b), b \approx 1 for K series
X-ray range about 0.01–10 nm; c; undeflected by fields

Chapter summary

  • Bohr kept the nuclear atom and added stationary states, mvr = nh/2\pi, and photon emission on a jump, hf = E_2 - E_1.
  • For hydrogen r_n = 0.529n^2 Å, v_n = 2.19\times10^6/n m s⁻¹ and E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV; the ground state is bound by 13.6 eV.
  • A downward jump n_2 \to n_1 emits 1/\lambda = R(1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2); each n_1 names a series.
  • Lyman ends on n = 1 and is ultraviolet; Balmer ends on n = 2 and is the only visible series; Paschen, Brackett and Pfund are infrared.
  • The number of lines from level n is n(n-1)/2; lines crowd to a series limit.
  • de Broglie: \lambda = h/p; an electron at 100 V has \lambda \approx 1.2 Å, small enough to diffract from crystals, which is the evidence for matter waves.
  • \Delta x\Delta p \ge h/4\pi: confinement increases momentum spread, which is why electrons cannot live in nuclei and why atomic orbits are not sharp paths.
  • X-rays come from a Coolidge tube: thermionic electrons accelerated onto a heavy target; over 99 % of the energy becomes heat.
  • The continuous spectrum is bremsstrahlung and cuts off at \lambda_{min} = hc/eV; the characteristic lines are inner-shell transitions and do not move with voltage. K_\alpha is never the shortest wavelength.
  • Bragg's law 2d\sin\theta = n\lambda measures crystal spacings; Moseley's \sqrt{f} = a(Z-b) makes the characteristic line an element fingerprint.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (b) — the allowed angular momenta are h/2\pi, 2h/2\pi, … so mvr = nh/2\pi. Option (a) misses the 2\pi.

2. (c) — r_n = 0.529n^2 Å, so the radius grows as the square of the quantum number.

3. (a) — E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV; the negative sign shows the electron is bound.

4. (d) — removing the electron from n=1 to n=\infty takes 0-(-13.6) = 13.6 eV.

5. (b) — the gap from n=1 to n=2 is 13.6(1-1/4) = 10.2 eV. The 3.4 eV in (a) is the ionisation energy from n=2.

6. (c) — every Lyman line ends on n=1, and the largest gaps give the shortest wavelengths, in the ultraviolet.

7. (a) — Balmer lines are jumps from higher levels down to n=2; that is why the visible hydrogen lines are Balmer lines.

8. (c) — Paschen lines end on n=3 and lie in the infrared.

9. (d) — the limit is the jump \infty \to 2: 1240/3.4 = 365 nm. The 656 nm in (c) is Hα, the first line, not the limit.

10. (a) — R = 1.097\times10^7 m⁻¹; (d) is cR, a frequency.

11. (b) — n=1 gives L = h/2\pi, not zero.

12. (d) — \lambda = h/p = h/mv; (b) is the inverse, which would have units of m⁻¹ s.

13. (c) — K = eV and \lambda = h/\sqrt{2mK}, so \lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{V}.

14. (b) — the product of the two uncertainties cannot be less than h/4\pi.

15. (a) — the tungsten filament is heated and electrons boil off it (thermionic emission).

16. (d) — bremsstrahlung: electrons lose any fraction of their energy on passing near a nucleus.

17. (c) — an inner-shell electron is knocked out, a higher electron falls in, and the fixed energy gap gives a sharp line.

18. (a) — \lambda_{min} = hc/eV contains only the voltage; the target sets the characteristic lines.

19. (b) — X-rays are photons, with no charge, so the Lorentz force on them is zero.

20. (d) — the extra path is 2d\sin\theta, measured from the planes.

21. (c) — \sqrt{f} = a(Z-b); the line frequency tracks atomic number.

22. (b) — a higher voltage gives each electron more energy, so shorter wavelengths and a harder beam. Filament current changes intensity, not hardness.

23. (a) — E = 1240/620 = 2.0 eV.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — an accelerating charge radiates; the electron would lose energy and spiral in within about 10^{-11} s, so atoms could not exist.

2. (a) — the smallest energy gap in a series gives the longest wavelength. 3\to2 is the smallest gap in Balmer; \infty\to2 gives the series limit, the shortest wavelength.

3. (d) — E_2 = -13.6/4 = -3.4 eV and E_1 = -13.6 eV, so E_2/E_1 = 1/4. Both are negative; the ratio is not 4.

4. (b) — r \propto n^2 so the radius is four times; v \propto 1/n so the speed is halved.

5. (c) — n(n-1)/2 = 4\times3/2 = 6: the jumps 4→1, 4→2, 4→3, 3→1, 3→2, 2→1.

6. (a) — 10.2 eV is exactly E_2 - E_1, so the atom is excited to n=2 and the photon is absorbed completely.

7. (d) — a photon is absorbed only if its energy equals a gap exactly. 11.0 eV is above the 10.2 eV gap but below 13.6 eV and matches no gap, so it passes by and the atom is unchanged.

8. (b) — \lambda = h/mv; at the same speed the lighter electron has the longer wavelength.

9. (c) — confining an electron to 10^{-14} m forces \Delta v \sim 6\times10^9 m s⁻¹, greater than c, which is impossible.

10. (a) — \lambda_{min} = hc/eV, so doubling V halves \lambda_{min}.

11. (d) — K_\beta falls from the M shell, a bigger energy gap than from L, so its photon has more energy and a shorter wavelength.

12. (c) — filament current sets the number of electrons, hence intensity; the wavelengths (including \lambda_{min}) are set by the voltage and the target.

13. (b) — 2d\sin\theta = n\lambda with fixed d and \lambda gives \sin\theta \propto n, so it doubles.

14. (a) — a high-Z target stops the electrons in a short distance and converts a larger fraction of their energy into X-rays, so the yield is higher.
